To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the characteristics of women who use hormone replacement therapy (ever-use versus non-compliant) and the duration of intake (long-term versus short-term) are associated with parity and age at first birth, hysterectomy, oophorectomies, education, exercise, food fiber intake, climacteric symptoms and oral contraceptives.
the characteristics of women using HRT vary with characteristics of their exposure.

the characteristics of hormone replacement therapy are important confounders of risk estimates for cardiovascular diseases and reproductive cancers, and that these confounders may be difficult to measure and control for.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the importance of selection bias in the interpretation of epidemiological studies on hormone replacement therapy (hrt) and its effects on major health risks.
the methodological problems of confounding and selection in epidemiology, and with the need for more refined exposure measures in studies of the effects of hormone replacement therapies.
the importance of selection biases in the interpretation of observational studies on HRT effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence of confounding in observational studies is strong and the risk estimates may be seriously biased.
the effects of HRT on cardiovascular diseases, osteoporosis and cancer are confounded by exposure characteristics, but the direction and magnitude of the bias is unknown.
HRT is a complex intervention that may affect a wide range of health outcomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HRT is a complex treatment, and that the choice of using it or not, and of using it long-term or not, is related to a number of factors that may confound associations between HRT and diseases.
the use of HRT is a marker of a healthy lifestyle and of a healthy body.
the risk of confounding by selection in observational studies of hormone replacement therapy is complex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the selection of HRT users may be associated with important risk determinants and that this may lead to confounding of HRT effects.
selection biases are important and complex.
selection bias may vary with the exposure and that it is important to consider exposure characteristics in studies on HRT.
